imports.name: GitHub
imports.why: Evidence explicitly says development of this public runtime project should use the reusable GitHub provider while its canonical remote is on github.com. This relationship is not among the already accepted STEP-07 assignments; Development Workflow is already assigned separately and is not re-emitted.

rules.statement: Before implementation, framework-context, or substantial documentation changes, ensure an Issue records why the change exists; it may be brief.
rules.title: Back every change with an Issue
rules.why: Repository history should show the reason without reconstructing chat history.

rules.statement: Before starting a new coherent development block, record a short purpose and checklist in the project's durable planning surface; use `PLAN.md` when the project follows this workflow convention.
rules.title: Plan a coherent change block before editing
rules.why: Repository state must explain what work is in progress even if the chat, model session, or tool run disappears.

rules.statement: When a listed step is actually complete, mark its `PLAN.md` checkbox `[x]` immediately rather than reconstructing completion at the end of a long session.
rules.title: Checkpoint completed plan items immediately
rules.why: Immediate checkpoints turn PLAN into a reliable recovery ledger instead of requiring plan archaeology after an interruption.

rules.statement: Put decisions, active constraints, accepted state, and next steps needed to resume work in repository documentation such as `PLAN.md`, `STATE.md`, or the project's equivalent rather than relying on chat history or model memory.
rules.title: Keep recovery-critical knowledge in the repository
rules.why: Long conversations and agent sessions are transient; the repository is the durable shared recovery point for humans and tools.

rules.statement: When the project owner resumes work after a short conversational interruption, explicitly says to continue, and reports no intervening repository changes, continue from the last established branch/PR state unless a repository operation gives evidence that it changed. Do not spend a new work cycle re-checking already established repository facts merely to prove that nothing happened.
rules.title: Resume recent explicit continuation without re-proving unchanged state
rules.why: In a controlled single-owner workflow, repeated defensive re-verification consumes the useful working window without adding evidence. Any stated or observed intervening change still invalidates this assumption.

rules.statement: When Markdown is also parsed, compiled, extracted, or otherwise given machine-significant meaning, every field or wording whose value affects machine semantics must live in an explicitly marked machine structure rather than being inferred from ordinary presentation prose. Keep that machine significance recognizable in rendered and review surfaces; rendering may style or summarize the control structure, but must not make the machine/human boundary indistinguishable.
rules.title: Mark machine-significant Markdown explicitly
rules.why: Humans must be able to tell which Markdown is freely editable presentation and which content participates in operational semantics; hidden parser contracts turn harmless-looking prose edits into surprising behavior.

rules.statement: For one coherent correction block, make the related authoring/code changes and run proportionate focused checks first; do not repeat the project's most expensive generated-output, integration, packaging, or full verification cycle after every micro-edit.
rules.title: Batch related edits before expensive final verification
rules.why: Final verification is valuable, but repeating it on superseded intermediate heads adds ceremony without increasing confidence in the candidate that will actually be reviewed or merged.

rules.statement: When the project owner explicitly approves a coherent implementation scope and says intermediate product review is unnecessary, mark the Fast Track as active in the durable PLAN with its scope and exit condition, keep recovery checkpoints and focused verification inside bounded work blocks, and defer repeated PR-description polish, full CI, generated-output regeneration, and other review ceremony until the coherent review candidate. When the Fast Track ends, record that closure before returning to ordinary review cadence.
rules.title: Use owner-approved Fast Track blocks without weakening the final gate
rules.why: Explicit delegation can remove intermediate coordination cost without sacrificing recoverability. Visible start/scope/exit/closure boundaries prevent a long single-worker Fast Track from becoming undocumented process state, while final human review and exact-head merge verification remain unchanged.

rules.statement: A coherent development block may be presented for project-owner review while understood and disclosed CI failures or generated drift remain. After explicit project-owner approval and before merging, require the exact current head to pass the project's complete merge-gate verification, including zero generated drift when generated canonical output is part of the project contract.
rules.title: Require exact-head green verification at the merge gate, not the first review gate
rules.why: Human review should happen before spending finalization effort on a candidate that may still change, while the accepted branch remains protected by a strict reproducibility gate.

rules.statement: When actively testing an installable Python tool from a development checkout, prefer one editable install (`uv tool install --editable .`) and pull subsequent revisions with Git rather than reinstalling each version, when the environment supports it.
rules.title: Prefer editable installs for repeated owner testing
rules.why: This keeps the owner-test loop short and makes the tested command follow the current checkout.

rules.statement: When an executable tool is tested from a changing Git checkout, keep its release version stable until a real release/version boundary, but make runtime version output identify the current VCS state with the branch/ref when available, commit identity, and dirty state. Treat the commit identity as authoritative and the branch/ref as human orientation; release artifacts without checkout metadata still report the canonical release version.
rules.title: Expose development provenance without micro-bumping releases
rules.why: Humans and agents must be able to distinguish different development code behind the same release baseline without turning every branch, documentation edit, or review iteration into release-version ceremony.

rules.statement: Applicable Context constrains a task; it does not silently expand its writable scope.
rules.title: Expand change scope explicitly
rules.why: A local task must not acquire wider impact merely because broader Context was loaded.

rules.statement: Keep a review PR or equivalent change set open until the project owner explicitly approves the reviewed result.
rules.title: Do not merge without explicit project-owner approval
rules.why: Green automation proves only the properties it checks; it does not prove that the product, architecture, or documentation is acceptable to its human owner.

rules.statement: After a reviewed change is successfully merged into the accepted branch, reconcile the durable repository state that records the accepted baseline before starting the next coherent development block. Record the merge outcome in `PLAN.md`, update `STATE.md` or equivalent current-state documentation, and refresh README/CHANGELOG or review-status wording made stale by the merge when applicable.
rules.title: Close the post-merge baseline checkpoint before new development
rules.why: The merge itself creates project facts after the merge candidate was frozen. Without a post-merge checkpoint, the accepted code can be correct while recovery documentation still describes the pre-merge state.

rules.statement: Manage workflow Issues, Pull Requests, reviews, checks/CI status, and merge state in the project's GitHub repository. Branches and commits remain ordinary Git objects; when a capable local harness is available, edit and test the local working tree directly rather than treating GitHub file APIs as a substitute filesystem.
rules.title: Use GitHub development objects
rules.why: The workflow should use standard GitHub semantics and tools while local code work stays local when possible.

rules.statement: Canonical Issue content lives in ordinary Markdown below `issues/`; caches or indexes may accelerate access later but must remain reconstructable.
rules.title: Keep project truth visible
rules.why: development reasoning is durable project knowledge, not opaque runtime state.

rules.statement: Use the local working tree and Git for branches, commits, diffs, and merges; do not proxy file operations through `github.local`.
rules.title: Use native Git for code state
rules.why: Git already solves these concerns locally and is the most compatible surface for IDE agents.

rules.statement: Unsupported or unavailable operations must fail explicitly instead of creating state on github.com or another provider.
rules.title: Never fall back to an external forge silently
rules.why: privacy-sensitive projects must not leak workflow state or acquire a second accidental source of truth.

rules.statement: Prefer stable command names, exit codes, and structured JSON output over interactive UI requirements.
rules.title: Keep the CLI model-friendly
rules.why: terminal-capable LLM harnesses need a predictable low-overhead contract.

rules.statement: Terminal-capable agents must be able to perform the normal workflow through stable CLI commands and structured output; MCP or other adapters are optional additions, not prerequisites.
rules.title: Keep the CLI as the primary agent contract
rules.why: the real corporate Copilot owner test succeeded without MCP and demonstrated that CLI calls provide a simple, low-overhead integration surface.

rules.statement: For capabilities that github.local supports, prefer official `gh` command vocabulary, flags, aliases, and user-facing defaults wherever they map cleanly to the local architecture; every deliberate deviation must be explicit, documented, and justified.
rules.title: Default to GitHub CLI compatibility
rules.why: humans and LLMs already trained on GitHub should be able to transfer that knowledge directly instead of learning accidental local syntax.

rules.statement: A folder owns an Issue backlog only after an explicit `github-local issue init`; local Issue-repository boundaries are independent of Git repository boundaries and may be nested.
rules.title: Make local Issue repositories explicit workflow boundaries
rules.why: A company, product, and independently managed extension can each be a GitHub-like unit of work without forcing nested Git repositories or mixing unrelated work into one label-heavy backlog.

rules.statement: Issue commands must require `-R/--repo`; `-R .` explicitly asks github.local to resolve the nearest initialized local Issue repository from that location. Never select a repository merely because of the process CWD.
rules.title: Require explicit Issue-repository selection for normal Issue work
rules.why: Humans and LLM agents both lose track of directory context. Making the target part of the command turns a likely silent misfile into an explicit decision that is visible in logs and prompts.

rules.statement: Each initialized folder owns a visible `issues/` store, its stable path-independent workflow repository ID, and local configuration. Inside Git, all nested Issue repositories share a short-number series per containing Git repository; Git-free folders allocate locally.
rules.title: Keep each local Issue repository an explicit, movable workflow boundary
rules.why: Products and extensions remain independently identifiable for future external mappings, while one Git project provides short unambiguous Issue references.

rules.statement: Initialization, teardown, Issue deletion, and bulk deletion must be available through github.local; destructive operations require confirmation unless the caller explicitly opts out.
rules.title: Keep destructive Issue administration explicit and CLI-owned
rules.why: Users and agents should never need to discover and manipulate hidden implementation files, while visible Markdown Issues remain intentionally inspectable project artifacts.

rules.statement: In Git, canonical Issues, comments and durable configuration belong to the currently checked-out branch/worktree and must be commit/push/clone-able with ordinary Git; never redirect to the primary worktree or silently exclude canonical data from Git.
rules.title: Couple Issue state to normal Git history
rules.why: The meaning of an Issue evolves with the code and project's Context. A historical commit must reproduce the corresponding historical Issue state, with normal PyCharm/Git semantics.

rules.statement: Every new Issue and comment has a separately generated immutable UUID in marked front matter. Within one Git repository allocate monotonically increasing short Issue numbers using a shared local lock/cursor; independent offline clones may temporarily allocate equal numbers. Comment Markdown filenames must start with a sortable per-Issue sequence and readable summary; a short UUID suffix prevents parallel Git branches from overwriting each other's comments.
rules.title: Separate immutable identity from short, human-readable identifiers
rules.why: People communicate using `#33` and browse discussions using `0001`, `0002`, `0003`; opaque UUID-only filenames and randomly ordered comments destroy that human workflow. The internal UUID, not the short display number, remains the technical identity.

rules.statement: Accept normal Git merges, detect different UUIDs bearing the same number, block unsafe writes, preview which Issue retains the number, and renumber others to unused integers only after confirmation. Preserve old numbers, dates and available branch provenance in the renamed Issue, and never guess the meaning of ambiguous text/commit/external references.
rules.title: Repair rare post-merge number collisions explicitly
rules.why: Occasional coordinated offline work should remain possible without burdening routine single-owner Git use with custom merge hooks or secondary history.

rules.statement: Use ordinary visible `.gitignore` only for locks/cursors/temporary files; never hide Issues or durable identity with `.git/info/exclude`. Provide a transparent, explicit legacy migration that preserves content and never stages/commits behind the user's back.
rules.title: Keep lasting state Git-trackable and migrate legacy stores safely
rules.why: A user who commits/pushes the project must not silently lose hundreds of valuable Issues because a support tool kept them outside Git.

rules.statement: Provide explicit close/reopen semantics and automatically close an Issue when accepted/merged work carries an explicit closing reference; do not treat an arbitrary Issue mention as a closing instruction.
rules.title: Let completed work leave the open backlog
rules.why: the open backlog should naturally shrink as accepted work completes while closure remains deliberate and inspectable.

rules.statement: Use the local working tree and native Git for branches, commits, diffs, and merges; do not proxy file operations through github.local.
rules.title: Use native Git for code state
rules.why: Git already owns code state locally and is the most compatible surface for IDE agents, while github.local owns workflow objects.

rules.statement: Keep canonical Issue content in ordinary Markdown below issues/; any cache or index must remain reconstructable.
rules.title: Keep canonical Issue truth visible
rules.why: Development reasoning is durable project knowledge, not opaque runtime state.

rules.statement: Unsupported or unavailable operations must fail explicitly instead of creating state on github.com or another provider.
rules.title: Never fall back to an external forge silently
rules.why: Privacy-sensitive projects must not leak workflow state or acquire a second accidental source of truth.

rules.statement: Keep normal workflow available through discoverable stable CLI commands, explicit error exits, and structured JSON; MCP and other adapters are optional additions, not prerequisites.
rules.title: Keep the CLI as the predictable primary agent contract
rules.why: Terminal-capable agents need a predictable low-overhead contract, and the target-environment owner test succeeded without MCP.

rules.statement: Within a Git project, code and Issue Markdown follow ordinary branches/worktrees together. UUIDs never duplicate; short numbers are unique within each integrated checkout and exceptionally reconciled after a merge of independently numbered clones.
rules.title: Keep workflow state coherent with its Git project snapshot
rules.why: Historical code and its semantic Issue context must match. The earlier branch-independent backlog direction was explicitly superseded by owner decision in Issue #20.

rules.statement: Provide explicit close and reopen semantics, and automatically close an Issue only when accepted or merged work carries an explicit closing reference.
rules.title: Let completed work leave the open backlog deliberately
rules.why: The open backlog should shrink as accepted work completes while closure remains deliberate and inspectable; an arbitrary mention is not a closing instruction.

rules.statement: Store each Issue as one Markdown file with a strict, delimited, machine-owned JSON front matter block; maintain its title and body once as Markdown.
rules.title: Mark Issue machine metadata explicitly
rules.why: Explicit metadata supports standard tooling without hiding parser semantics or duplicating human content.

rules.statement: Allocate monotonically increasing Issue numbers per containing Git repository using a shared Git-local OS lock/cursor across local branches and worktrees; Git-free Issue repositories allocate locally. Publish content with same-directory atomic replacement.
rules.title: Serialize shared local numbering and publish Issues atomically
rules.why: Rapid local creation must not duplicate numbers or expose partial files; separately cloned offline histories can be reconciled after Git integration.

rules.statement: If a database is added, use it only as an index or cache rebuildable from issues/ and Git state.
rules.title: Treat databases as rebuildable indexes
rules.why: Canonical project truth must remain visible and reconstructable without opaque runtime state.

rules.statement: Build optional gh-compatible, MCP, IDE, or UI adapters on the same application service and canonical storage; adapter concerns must not contaminate Issue files.
rules.title: Keep optional adapters outside canonical storage
rules.why: Presentation and compatibility surfaces may evolve independently while durable project semantics remain stable.

rules.statement: Identify and configure the local project through repository discovery without network discovery.
rules.title: Keep repository discovery local
rules.why: The provider must remain usable as a local workflow surface without depending on a service or external host.

rules.statement: Each Issue's UUID is its sole permanent technical identity. Its short numeric filename prefix is a human communication handle, normally stable but exceptionally renumbered after a confirmed offline-merge collision; the Windows-safe slug is presentation and may change with the title.
rules.title: Use immutable Issue IDs and human-friendly mutable numbers
rules.why: Renumbering must preserve the underlying Issue and its historical discussion without changing identity.
